problem: Prior navigation work passes non-visual guidance (waypoint vectors, GPS, LiDAR, text) to the agent as a separate modality, so the agent must learn to map that signal onto its image observations. This is hard in dynamic scenes and makes sim-to-real transfer difficult.
motivation: Deep networks are good at extracting relations inside images, so rendering navigation cues directly onto the visual observation could remove the burden of fusing modalities. Semantic segmentation is a domain-invariant mid-level representation, so rendering guidance on it may also allow zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, similar to Google Maps AR guidance for humans.
key_idea: Render navigation guidance (colored paths or waypoint spheres) directly onto the semantic-segmentation observation of a DRL agent, in simulation and via AR in the real world, instead of feeding vector guidance.
insight: Inside the same segmentation-based agent, image-space guidance beats vector guidance (SegVec) in all three simulated scenarios. The error analysis shows the gain comes mainly from far fewer out-of-bound failures (1.8% vs 11.8%), while collisions are unchanged. Denser guidance works better: waypoints only (57.7 SPL) < path S→D (67.5) < real-time path P_t→waypoint (68.6). Using pseudo scene coordinates rendered from the SfM mesh gives more accurate waypoint placement than the SCR-estimated coordinates, but this is shown only qualitatively.
method: Planning module: A* plans paths S→D, P_t→waypoints or P_t→D, either one-time at episode start or real-time each step; agent position is known in simulation and estimated by SCR in the real world.
Virtual guidance representation: the planned path is rendered as a 3D colored mesh path or as regularly spaced 3D spheres (waypoints) and projected onto the semantic-segmentation image.
DRL agent: SAC agent taking 3 stacked 84x180 segmentation frames, at constant speed 6 m/s, with steering actions; reward = navigation reward (waypoint collected / on path) + goal reward (+10 / -10).
Language-to-guidance: GPT-4 with few-shot prompts turns instructions into sub-goal object descriptions, and YOLO-World detects them zero-shot in the image.
Visual re-localization with SCR (ACE-style): trained on SfM pseudo-poses with a reprojection loss; PnP gives the camera pose.

Two-stage waypoint placement: after obtaining the pose from SCR+PnP, pseudo scene coordinates are rendered from the Poisson-reconstructed SfM mesh and looked up at detection boxes to get 3D waypoints, which are then rendered as AR guidance.
Sim-to-real: the real segmentation (Rainbow, 12 classes) and guidance are rendered with the same color set as in simulation, and the frozen policy is deployed on a Clearpath Husky.

setting.backbone: SAC DRL agent (CNN on segmentation frames, trained from scratch); GPT-4 (frozen, few-shot) and YOLO-World (frozen) for language grounding; SCR model (ACE-style) and Rainbow segmentation
setting.training_data: RL in custom Unity ML-Agents environments; Hard scenario: 89 training routes; 3 random seeds; SCR trained on images from the target real scene with SfM pseudo-poses
setting.observation: 3 stacked 84x180 semantic segmentation frames with rendered virtual guidance (real world: monocular RGB converted to segmentation plus AR overlay)
setting.action_space: steering: keep heading or change angular acceleration by ±35°/s² (kappa=2) at constant 6 m/s
setting.privileged: Simulation: the planner knows the agent position P_t. Real world: none beyond the pre-built SfM/SCR model of the scene.

numbers_note: Custom Unity benchmarks, not standard ones. Table 1 reports mean±std over seeds (std not copied here). Hard-scenario numbers appear in both Table 1 and Table 3. The pseudo vs. estimated scene coordinate comparison is qualitative only (figure).
results: In all three simulated scenarios, virtual guidance beats the SegVec vector baseline. In Hard, SPL is 67.5 vs 48.9 and SR 67.8 vs 52.1, and out-of-bound failures drop from 11.8% to 1.8%. The policy transfers to a real Husky robot without fine-tuning with 73–80% SR, including language-instructed routes.
limitations: Evaluated only on custom Unity environments against a single self-designed baseline (SegVec), with no standard benchmarks; real-world tests are small (30 runs) and SR is lower than in simulation.
Relies on a pre-built SfM/SCR model of the target scene, an accurate segmentation model, and given object-based sub-goals; the two-stage placement claim is only qualitative.
Collision rate is unchanged by virtual guidance (21.0% vs 21.6%), and the simulation planner assumes known agent position.
builds_on: mid-level representations for sim-to-real (Hong et al. 2018, Yang et al. 2022)
